accuracy.reason: Cards 1-3 accurately scope a database-backed cache as a reusable copy, explain hit/miss cost and application-owned cache-aside, and require answer-distinguishing keys. Cards 4-5 correctly deny freshness from deletion or TTL and separate expiration from capacity eviction. Cards 6-8 preserve failure and workload limits.

evidence.quote: First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.

mechanisms.reason: Every card has a causal mechanism: reuse saves repeated work; API owns fills; old in-flight values can refill after deletion; TTL and eviction remove without fetching; local copies diverge; shared outages broaden lost access; coalescing and bounded fallback reduce source demand. Final measurement connects mechanism to value.

evidence.quote: A hit avoids this database lookup. A miss still needs the database.

coherence.reason: API/database and concurrency prerequisites suffice. Cards proceed from benefit and read flow to ownership, overlapping writes, entry lifetime, topology, overload and decision. Inspected hit/miss and stale-price diagrams assign work correctly and do not imply freshness; shared renderer/CSS already inspected, no execution claimed.

evidence.quote: Define what the key identifies, who fills it, and where the authoritative data lives.

decisions.reason: Cards 6-8 compare copy visibility, network cost and failure scope, teach cold/outage testing and bounded database fallback, and reject low-reuse caching. Freshness-sensitive decisions stay tied to authoritative data; hit ratio, latency and source load evaluate benefit.

evidence.quote: Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. To avoid charging an old price at checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.

clarity.reason: Terms are introduced with concrete operations: keys distinguish currencies, old price refill demonstrates the race, and entry disappearance distinguishes expiration and eviction. The short decision checklist retains costs and limits without an unexplained protocol.

evidence.quote: TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

outcomes.reason: Learner connects repeated 80ms station-language construction to 2ms hits, includes station and language in the key, identifies API-owned lookup/fetch/fill/return and retains miss, write, storage and freshness costs.

Learner traces A refilling old hours after B deletion, rejects post-write freshness, and proposes direct authoritative reads for this endpoint. This supported bypass satisfies the required simple remedy.

Learner correctly identifies stale 12:03 hit, expired 12:11 miss and evicted 12:05 miss; TTL neither refreshes nor guarantees presence. Application fetching on the later miss and explicit rejection of automatic refresh distinguish removal from refilling.

Learner explains untouched old local copies and chooses the shared entry under no-concurrent-fill assumptions, contrasting in-process/network access, operation cost and one-instance versus all-instance lost cache access; no automatic freshness or application-failure claim.

Learner explains concurrent duplicate refill reads and coalesces them into shared in-progress work. It compares 10000 demand with 500 source capacity, bounds total fallback and rejects excess. Optional stale data is explicitly conditional on an independently accessible copy and 60-second allowance.

Learner rejects filling single-use unique results: no future reuse, 2ms reads and ample capacity do not justify cache cost. It names operations/storage/maintenance, and requires repeated expensive or capacity-constrained reads plus acceptable staleness before reconsidering.

sourceChecks.claim: Live Azure caching guidance supports repeated-read benefit, transient copies and persistent source of truth, with volatility and operating costs qualified.
Live Azure cache-aside steps assign cache lookup, source fetch and cache fill to the application; misses retain source work and consistency is not guaranteed.
Live Azure guidance and cache-aside sensitive-data example support keys distinguishing results and users, not universal automatic source tracking.

Live cache-aside consistency limitations support stale copies; the supplied explicit interleaving independently shows a paused old fill can occur after removal. Authoritative checkout validation avoids trusting this copy.
Live Redis eviction reference distinguishes memory policy, LRU, TTL-marked keys and noeviction errors. Expiration controls lifetime and cache-aside supplies the later fetch, not automatic refresh.
Live AWS caching discussion confirms divergent on-box copies, separate shared service, network/operational costs and broad shared-cache unavailability.
Live AWS discussion confirms coalescing to one pending resource request, outage-induced downstream surge, rate caps/load shedding and disabled-cache tests.
Live Azure guidance supports choosing frequently reused costly results with tolerated volatility and performance/usage measurement; low reuse can cost more than it saves.
